glossary.Airflow obstruction: Narrowing of the airways so air cannot be breathed out quickly.
glossary.Wheeze: A whistling sound, mainly on breathing out, caused by narrowed airways.
glossary.Chronic cough: A cough lasting more than 8 weeks.
glossary.Reduced breath sounds: Quieter sounds heard through the stethoscope, as with over-inflated lungs or poor air entry.
glossary.Respiratory failure: When the lungs cannot keep blood oxygen up or carbon dioxide down to safe levels.
glossary.Lung function: How well the lungs move air, usually measured by spirometry such as FEV1.
glossary.Peak flow variability: How much peak flow readings change over the day or between days; high variability suggests asthma.
glossary.Long-acting bronchodilators: Inhalers such as LABAs and LAMAs that keep the airways open for about 12 to 24 hours.
glossary.Bronchodilator: A drug that relaxes airway muscle to widen the airways.
glossary.Smoking cessation: Stopping smoking, the only measure that slows lung function decline in COPD.
glossary.Controlled oxygen: Oxygen at a set low concentration, targeting sats 88 to 92% in people at risk of CO2 retention.
glossary.Steroids: Anti-inflammatory drugs, such as oral prednisolone in an exacerbation.
glossary.Antibiotics: Drugs that kill bacteria, given in an exacerbation if there are signs of bacterial infection.
glossary.Bronchospasm: Sudden tightening of the muscle around the airways, narrowing them.
glossary.Neutrophils: White blood cells that drive the inflammation of COPD and are less steroid-responsive.
glossary.Structural damage: Permanent changes to the lung, such as destroyed alveoli, that drugs cannot reverse.
glossary.Phenotype: The observable type of a disease in a patient, such as eosinophilic asthma.
glossary.Eosinophilic asthma: A type of asthma driven by eosinophils that responds well to steroids.
glossary.Atopic: Having a tendency to allergic conditions such as asthma, eczema and hay fever.
glossary.Fixed obstruction: Airway narrowing that does not improve with a bronchodilator.
